cells.tense: Right now you are holding what can keep growing by releasing what is done, and the shape of it is in your hand.
cells.act: weigh what it costs them against what it gives
cells.ask: Take something you carry on someone's behalf, set its true weight on both sides — what it asks of them, what it returns — and follow where the scale tips.
cells.core:
What you tend keeps growing because you let the dead parts drop. In the clearing where what matters is sensed before it is understood, you can see which piece of the work or the household is spent and which is still alive, and the spent one gets composted without ceremony. Whoever you're keeping it for gets the fruit, not the funeral.

Fairness has become something you can do on purpose. This week, take something you carry on someone's behalf and set it on the scale honestly — what it asks of them, what it returns. Don't ask them to reassure you. Make the fair call and let it stand where they can see it. The clearing stays honest when you keep your own accounts, and the growth you're stewarding keeps belonging to the ones it feeds.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what's spent and what's still growing.
cells.verb: holding and shaping what can keep growing by knowing what to let go and what to keep
cells.place: a clearing where what matters is sensed before it is understood

cells.tense: You will be composting what hasn't finished yet, forcing the ground before it has grown anything worth keeping.
cells.act: ask how it feels to them and stay with the answer
cells.ask: Ask someone your next change will touch what it's like on their side of it, then stay there a minute without explaining, fixing, or deciding.
cells.core:
On the stone step before the harvest, you are already turning under what hasn't ripened. The clear eye that knows what to release has started seeing endings everywhere, and they're being made before the thing has had its season. From where you stand it looks like stewardship. From the field, the rule reads as: nothing stays young here for long.

What's thin is standing alongside them, not deciding. Pick someone your change touches and ask what it's like on their side of it. Then stay with that for a minute — no explaining, no fixing. Let what they feel sit on the scale next to what you see. The next turn of the soil will be the right one, and less often.
cells.sheetLine: You're composting what hasn't finished growing.

cells.tense: A season has already turned and you are still standing at the gate of the last one, waiting for it to open.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Give your motivation a small steady portion: choose one piece of what you've been leaving for later, take a single step into it today, then stop.
cells.core:
The field is ready and the tools are by the gate, but you're at the gate and not in the field. You can still sense what matters — that part hasn't gone — and it isn't landing on anything living. The hours go to keeping old ground tidy instead of feeding new ground, and that is why the season feels stuck.

Give your motivation a small steady portion. Find one piece of what you've been leaving for later — something outside the dead ground — and take a single step into it today. Then stop. The step isn't the point. The point is the fire getting a little movement through it without being asked to burn a whole field. Steady, a bit at a time, is how the gate finally ends up behind you.
cells.sheetLine: The ground is ready and you're still at the gate.

cells.place: a clearing where what matters is sensed before it is understood

cells.tense: You are already the one deciding what gets kept and what goes, and the pen has been in your hand the whole time.
cells.act: lead the change by moving first
cells.ask: Name one change you've been waiting on someone else to start, then go first on it yourself — a single decisive move, no announcement.
cells.core:
You've been shaping what grows here for a while, and your own account has you as a caretaker of something that was already there. Ask who released the old things, whose hand chose what got kept, and the answer comes back as: nobody really decided. But the shape of this place is your work, and it will tell you so if you listen.

What isn't on the table yet is your name on it. Name one change you've been waiting for someone else to start — the boundary, the cut, the lead — and go first on it yourself. One decisive move, no announcement. The ground will still look like ground. The difference is that you'll know you made it, and the next call will come easier.
cells.sheetLine: You've been choosing what grows here. Sign it.
